Maine State Museum Testimony Re: LD 1614

Testimony from Bernard Fishman to the joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, Regarding LD 1614, a bill to Facilitate the Ability of the Maine State
Museum to Acquire and Preserve Special Collections.

Sen. Rafferty, Rep. Murphy, and honorable members ofthe Joint Standing Committee on
Education and CulturalAffairs, I am Bernard Fishman, director of the Maine State Museum, and I am here to offertestimony concerning LD 1614, a bill to `Facilitate the Ability ofthe Maine State Museum to Acquire and Preserve Special Collections.' I will offer my
comments as being neither for nor against the passage of this bill.
This well-intentioned and forward-looking proposal is based on a genuine need, namely
that the Maine State Museum does not have sufficient good~quality collection storage space to accommodate present and future growth in its collections. In saying this I must recognize and express my gratitude to the present administration, the legislature, and
especially to the Bureau of General Services (BGS) under DAFS, for making additional
storage space available to the museum some three years ago, in connection with the
renovation of the Cultural Building in Augusta. DAFS renovated portions of the Center Building, a disused structure once part of the old AMHI facility on the east side of the |<ennnebec, to make it available for subsequent storage use. This was, however, the first
significant addition to museum storage space in decades, and the museum does not yet
have sufficient climate-controlled, clean, dry, and accessible storage for the 800,000
objects presently in its collections, let alone future additions. One result is that the
museum must sometimes consider declining significant potential donations because
there is not the space, or not the right space, to properly accommodate them and care for them into the long future.
The lack of sufficient museum-grade storage for collections is a problem that many successful museums have. My understanding from BGS is that there is no state facility now
available that could be renovated to provide additional collection storage needs forthe
museum, and that therefore only new construction could satisfy that requirement, which at
today's prices would be $ 500 per square foot, and would represent a major $ 4.5 million
commitment. One does not have to be a soothsayer to recognize that such a large expenditure is unlikely to be undertaken at this particular financial moment in the state's
history.

But many states have invested in modern storage facilities to properly preserve heritage
collections, and often those facilities include, for the sake of efficiency and cooperation,
the collections of several state-operated cultural entities wor|<ing together in the same facility. Herein Maine, the State Museum, of course, but also Maine's Bureau of Parks and
Lands, and the Maine Historic Preservation Commission, would surely benefit from having a joint storage facility for collections care, where important collections could be collectively preserved and researchers served.
While this might not be the time to consider such a facility, and forgive me forthis suggestion, seeing as I am inexperienced in working with most of you and with some of our
state systems, perhaps one way to begin to address this space issue would be to wor|< with DAFS overthe next year or more to create a master plan that would address the collection
and preservation needs of the museum and other state agencies that have key historical
holdings. As I have mentioned to this committee on previous occasions, though the state of
Maine has been a good supporter of the museum and of our basic needs, the museum has
over time developed mainly through opportunistically available facilities and augmentations, but has never had an effective, comprehensive, and pursued master plan to mark its expected development and guide its future facilities needs and growth. Perhaps
the bill before you could be amended to encourage the museum and DAFS to together
create such a master plan, which would be forward-looking, administratively thoughtful, and in keeping with the spirit of this bill. Developing such a plan would acknowledge
Maine's pride in its impressive and inspiring historical heritage, which we can all, without
exception, agree should be preserved in keeping with its great and lasting importance.

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs

Good afternoon, Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. I am Representative Dan Shagoury, and I
represent House District 55 -- the connnunities of Hallowell, Manchester and West Gardiner. I
am pleased to introduce LD 1614, Resolve, to Facilitate the Ability of the Maine State
Museum to Acquire and Preserve Special Collections.

I am submitting this bill on behalf of a constituent, Steve Thompson, who has a truly remarkable collection on Maine-related harness racing memorabilia. He will be speaking after me, and I will
leave it to him to describe the collection, but I have seen it and it is very impressive and I feel it
is worth keeping intact for future generations of Mainers.

We had discussions with the museum, but one reason they couldn't fully consider it was because
they simply didn't have the right space for such a large collection. I find that a real shame. Not just because of this collection in particular, although I do find it be historically significant. I feel that way more because I am sure there are other collections around the state that really do, as they say "belong in a museum."

Now, I am not a professional, so it is not up to me to tell the museum that they have to take this,
or any other particular collection. They are the professionals, and that is their call. I put this bill in to give them the option of taking a truly significant collection, should the opportunity come
up.

I have heard that the official position is that there is no space available and that new space would have to be built. I certainly don't want that, but I have a hard time believing that there is "no
space." What I would really like for this committee to do is to direct DAF S to provide a list of unused space the state has. It can be space that may need a little work, like the old DHHS building or some of the unused buildings at the old AMHI campus, but it would be good to know

Good afternoon Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of
the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs. I am
Stephen Thompson, the founder and creative director of The Lost Trotting Parks Heritage Center, a 501 C3 Nonprofit.
(NOTE: Beginning in 2009, I started collecting harness racing memorabilia. The memorabilia was used to create content for blogs, a Website and banners that were mounted on
the top of my Dad's 1967 Chevy C-10 Pickup with 10 panels to tell the story of the sport
of harness racing. In 2012/13, a nonprofit called The Lost Trotting Parks Heritage Center was formed to promote the the history and the sport of harness racing and other horse competitions. As a nonprofit the memorabilia increased. In November of this year,
I will turn 77. This collection is too valuable not to find a secure home for the collection which would serve as the basis for creating a Museum or History Room titled, "In Celebration of the Horse." Individuals who contribute to the Archive may still need to have access to the materials in order that they can still maintain the work they had been doing. If it is just a personal collection there may be no need for access.)
My Work involves the Standardbred horse, harness racing, and the horse be-
ginning in the 18th century to present day. There is a rich history that could be lost. Oral history associated with harness racing unless it has been record-
ed is in danger. The story of Nelson 4209 and his owner C.H. Nelson of
Waterville although displayed at the Waterville History Society disappeared
in oral history. Clark Thompson, rediscovered Nelson 4209 when he was
1

researching the harness racing archives in the Special
Collections Room at the Folger Library at the University of Maine. Added to
the collection a number of years ago were the photos of track photographer, Guy Kendall. There are more than 90 communities in Maine where trotting parks existed
between 1882 and 1930. Many of Maine's historical societies still have
memorabilia of their fairs and harness racing. For at least 10 years I have worked as one of the Video Patrol Officers during
harness racing season. This position has allowed me to become friends with many of the men and women who work in the harness racing industry. As a
photographer, I have taken more than 40,000 photos of harness racing at the Maine Agricultural Fairs and at Maine's private tracks. Becoming part of this industry I have become part of its history, but documented its history through research and memorabilia collected throughout the years.
As we age, collectors of harness racing memorabilia may begin to wonder what will happen to their collections. In many instances when a person
passes away there collection are often forgotten or even just taken to the
dump. It is amazing the number of people who do remember the names of horses, their owners, trainers and drivers. However, this history may be forgotten as we age.
The creation of a 9,000 square foot space for special collections that would include harness racing would be of great value. Today's Maine newspaper
seldom published anything related to harness racing. Perhaps it is time for sports editors to re-evaluate their coverage of the sport of harness racing and other horse related competitive events.
The Lost Trotting Parks Heritage Center has an extensive collection of books, periodicals, harness racing programs and storyboards created with donated images and periodicals.

The Balch Race was to be the rematch between Nelson 4209 and Alcryon. An article in a Hallowell
newspaper prior to the race indicated that many Mainers would be in attendance and that fortunes would be made and lost on this race. Rumors swirled the night before the race -- the fix was on. Nelson did not want to drive Nelson 4209. He had secured the services of Budd Doble, but Doble baclc out at the last moment. Nelson attempted to secure the services of John Splan. Oddly, Splan had been paid $500.00 by Noble just to walk about the grounds
on the day of the race. A news article published after the race reported that Alcryon had been shoed with
heavier shoes that would result in brealr_ing throughout the race. Nelson won the race in three heats.

John Splan in his testimony reported that he had been paid to not drive, but also stated that he saw nothing in the performances of the horses that indicated any wrongdoing. Nelson refused to identify his business associate. Nelson and his famous
stallion were barred from all NTA tracks. Initially, Noble, Alon/on's manag er, refused to cooperate, but
eventually admitted the fraud. Balch, a horse trader and promoter of the race, committed suicide due to
